entities.name: Althing, the world's oldest surviving parliament, is established at Þingvellir
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Althing (Alþingi) is the national parliament of Iceland, established in 930 CE, making it the world's oldest surviving parliament in continuous operation. Meeting annually at Þingvellir (Parliament Plains) beside a dramatic rift valley, it was the governing assembly of the Icelandic Commonwealth (930-1262 CE) before Iceland fell under Norwegian and later Danish rule.

The Althing was established by Icelandic settlers — primarily Norse Vikings and Celtic slaves brought from the British Isles — as an outdoor assembly meeting for two weeks each summer at midsummer. It combined legislative, judicial, and executive functions: the Law Speaker (Lögsögumaður) memorized and recited the laws, the Lögrétta enacted legislation, and regional courts heard disputes. The conversion of Iceland to Christianity in 1000 CE was decided by vote at the Althing — one of history's most consequential democratic decisions.

The Althing lost power as Iceland came under Norwegian control in 1262, was dissolved under Danish rule in 1800, and reestablished in Reykjavík in 1844. Iceland's 1944 independence from Denmark and the establishment of the republic were proclaimed at Þingvellir, reconnecting modern Iceland to its ancient democratic tradition. The site is now a UNESCO World Heritage site and Iceland's most sacred national location.
